opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is that the teacher isn't just giving you the same data again — it's giving you a much richer training signal on that data. When you train from scratch on next-token prediction, every position gives you a one-hot target: this was the token that happened to appear. But the teacher gives you a full distribution over the vocabulary at every position. So it's telling you not just "the answer is X," but "X is most likely, Y is plausible, Z is basically impossible." That's what Hinton called dark knowledge, and in the language model setting it's a huge amount of extra information per token.

There's also a variance reduction angle. Natural text is noisy — the token that actually appears is one sample from some underlying distribution, and the student has to average over a lot of examples to figure out what that distribution is. The teacher has already done a lot of that averaging, so the student gets a smoothed, lower-variance target. Effectively you're getting more bits of supervision per example, which is why it looks a lot like having more data.

And then there's a capacity and learnability piece that I find really interesting. The teacher's distribution is something a neural network actually produced, so in some sense it's easier for another neural network to fit than raw human data, which can contain things that are just really hard or idiosyncratic. The student doesn't have the capacity to model everything, and the teacher implicitly tells it where to put its probability mass.

That connects to some of the work we did on on-policy distillation. Standard distillation trains the student on sequences the teacher or the dataset produced, but at inference time the student generates its own tokens and can drift into states it never saw during training — the classic exposure bias problem. If you instead let the student generate and have the teacher give feedback on the student's own outputs, you close that train-test mismatch, and you can also choose divergences, like reverse KL, that are mode-seeking rather than forcing a small model to cover every mode of a much bigger one. That tends to matter a lot when the capacity gap is large.

So the short version is: same data, but far denser and better-shaped supervision, and if you do it on-policy, supervision on the distribution the student will actually face.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the observed one-hot token target with the teacher’s full vocabulary distribution, including plausible alternatives such as Y.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'd say my understanding has shifted over time. The classic story goes back to Hinton's "dark knowledge" paper, where the idea is that the teacher's soft distribution over tokens carries way more information per example than the single ground-truth token you get from the data. If the next word is "dog," the teacher is also telling you that "puppy" and "hound" were plausible and "refrigerator" was not. So every training example is effectively giving the student a whole gradient's worth of structure about the task rather than one bit, and you can think of it as a much richer, lower-variance training signal.

But honestly, I think that explanation is incomplete for language models, and the more interesting part is about the data distribution itself. When you train from scratch on raw web text, the student is trying to fit a target that is genuinely very hard, maybe harder than the student needs. Human-written data is multimodal, it's noisy, it has all these idiosyncrasies, and a small model with limited capacity ends up spending that capacity trying to model things it can't actually model well. Distillation, especially when you do it on-policy, where the student generates its own samples and the teacher scores or corrects them, changes the target into something that is more learnable. You're smoothing the distribution. The teacher has already done the work of compressing the messy world into a cleaner function, and the student is now fitting that cleaner function.

The other piece that I think is underappreciated is this train-inference mismatch. If you train a small model purely on fixed data with next-token prediction, at inference time it drifts into states it never saw during training, and it has no idea what to do there. With on-policy distillation, the student is being trained on its own mistakes, in exactly the states it will actually visit. The teacher acts like a dense reward signal at every single token, which is enormously more sample-efficient than, say, RL with a sparse reward at the end of the sequence.

So the way I'd summarize it is that it's really three things stacked together: more information per sample, a smoother and more learnable target, and a training distribution that matches what the student will actually face at deployment. And I think the honest answer is that we don't have a clean theory that quantifies how much each of those contributes. Empirically, though, the gap between a distilled student and a from-scratch student of the same size has been pretty consistent and pretty large, and that's what makes me think it's not just one mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the teacher’s soft distribution identifies alternatives such as “puppy” and “hound” as plausible when the observed next word is “dog,” going beyond the single ground-truth token.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the same data doesn’t necessarily mean the same learning signal. When you train from scratch on text, you observe one next token. But there might be many reasonable next tokens, and that single observation doesn’t tell you much about those alternatives.

A teacher can provide a much richer signal: which alternatives are plausible, how likely they are, and which ones are clearly wrong. So the student isn’t having to discover all of that structure independently. The larger model has already done some of that work, and distillation makes that structure easier for a smaller model to learn.

There’s also a distinction between matching the teacher’s probabilities and training on text generated by the teacher. In the second case, the benefit can come from the teacher producing examples that are cleaner or easier to learn from. So I wouldn’t say distillation automatically gives you a better student, but it can turn the available data into a more useful learning signal for the capacity that student has.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the single observed next token in text training with a teacher’s richer signal about which alternative tokens are plausible, likely, or wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the same data doesn’t necessarily mean the same learning signal. When you train from scratch, you typically show the model one observed next token and ask it to predict that token. But there could be several perfectly reasonable continuations.

A larger teacher gives you a distribution over those possibilities. That tells the student not just what the answer was, but which alternatives are plausible and how they relate to one another. The teacher has already learned structure that the student would otherwise have to discover from these individual observations.

So distillation can make the learning problem easier for a smaller model. It can spend its limited capacity approximating a useful function instead of having to find that function from scratch. That doesn’t guarantee a better student—the teacher can pass along mistakes, too—but it explains why matching the training data alone doesn’t make the two procedures equivalent.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the single observed next token in scratch training with a teacher’s distribution over plausible continuations, which gives the student supervision about alternatives.
